meaning: Youngest Titan, personification of time, who castrated and deposed his father Uranus before being overthrown by his son Zeus

phonemes.desc: Voiceless velar stop [k] followed by rolling rho.
Short omicron with acute pitch stress — the peak of the Titan's name.
Nu-omicron-sigma, a firm closing, almost a knell.

pronunciation.approximation: "KROH-nohs" — first syllable like "crow" without the w, second like "nose".

pronunciation.note: Krónos is Tier 2 because the Greek Κρόνος preserves only stress (acute on the first omicron), not length. The name's etymology is disputed; the acute marks the pitch peak, while the short vowels keep the name compact and hard, fitting a god whose story is one of cutting and devouring.

domains.title: The Youngest Titan
domains.subtitle: Harvest, Time, Sovereignty
domains.lead: Krónos is the youngest of the first-generation Titans, but he is the one who acts. He takes the sickle his mother gives him and cuts the sky. He swallows his children to stop time from replacing him. He rules a Golden Age that ends the moment his last son is born.

cards.name: The Sickle
cards.desc: The curved adamant blade with which he castrated Ouranos — the same shape that cuts grain at harvest.

cards.name: The Harvest
cards.desc: The Athenian Kronia linked him to grain and the year's abundance; the sickle is a reaper's tool before it is a weapon.

cards.name: The Throne
cards.desc: Kingship over gods and men during the mythic Golden Age, before the war that cast him down.

cards.name: The Devourer
cards.desc: He swallowed his children whole to defeat the prophecy of his overthrow — and swallowed a stone instead of Zeus.

symbols.name: Sickle/Harpē
symbols.meaning: The instrument of usurpation and harvest — one curved blade cuts the sky and the grain alike

symbols.name: Serpent
symbols.meaning: His kinship with the old chthonic powers; the devouring snake that seizes its prey whole is his animal

symbols.name: Golden grain
symbols.meaning: The wheat of the lost Golden Age, when earth bore fruit of itself and no one hungered

symbols.name: Swallowed stone
symbols.meaning: His single moment of blindness — the decoy that Rhea fed him, later the omphalos at Delphi

symbols.name: Scythe
symbols.meaning: The later, longer blade he acquired after the conflation with Time — from Saturn's sickle to Death's scythe

mythology.lead: Krónos is the hinge between the primordial gods and the Olympian order. His myth is the myth of generational succession — the son who overthrows the father and is in turn overthrown — and it is one of the most widely travelled stories in the ancient world.

myths.title: The Castration of Ouranos
myths.text: When Ouranos hid his and Gaia's children inside their mother, Gaia fashioned a great sickle of grey adamant and appealed to her sons. Hesiod records the decisive detail: ‘all of them were glad in their hearts to hear the words of Gaia's treacherous speech — all, that is, but great-hearted Kronos, the crooked of counsel, who was the youngest’; the others feared their father, but Kronos the youngest dared (Theogony 166–172). Gaia hid him in ambush; when Ouranós came at evening and spread himself over Gaia, Kronos stretched out his left hand and in his right took the great long sickle with jagged teeth, and swiftly cut off his own father's genitals and cast them behind him (Theogony 173–182). From the falling blood came the Erinyes, the Giants, and the Meliai; from the foam where the members fell, Aphrodítē. Even defeated, Ouranós names his sons Titanes, ‘strainers’, for their strained ambition (Theogony 207–210). The myth means that every Greek regime begins in a crime the victor does not regret: Kronos does what the others fear, and inherits the world for it.

myths.title: The Swallowed Children
myths.text: Power taught Kronos its oldest lesson: do to your children what was done to your father. Warned by Gaia and starry Ouranós that he was fated ‘to be overthrown by his own son, strong though he was’, he kept constant watch, and Rhéā bore him Hestía, Deméter, Hēra, Hádēs, and Poseidôn — each of whom he swallowed whole, straight from the holy womb (Theogony 453–467; Apollodorus 1.1.5–7). The belly became his fortress: the children did not grow old inside him, imprisoned in the living darkness of their father's stomach. When Zeus was born, Rhéā turned the trick: a stone in swaddling bands went down Kronos's throat instead, and the youngest son grew up in a Cretan cave. The myth means that devouring is a failed form of immortality — Kronos could swallow the future but could not digest it, and what he swallowed he eventually had to give back.

myths.title: The Titanomachy
myths.text: The decade-long war that decided cosmic government is the largest single episode of the Theogony (617–735). Zeus grew to manhood in Crete, took the Oceanid Mētis as counselor — she gave Kronos the emetic that made him disgorge the swallowed children, ‘the stone last of all’, which Zeus set up as a wonder and sign at Pytho (Apollodorus 1.1.7–1.2.1) — and then opened war on the Titans. For ten years the battle hung even, ‘with no advantage on either side’, until Zeus descended into the depths and freed the Cyclopes, who armed him with the thunderbolt, and the Hundred-Handers, whose hundred rock-showered arms overwhelmed the Titan line. The defeated Titans were bound in painful chains and cast beneath the wide-pathed earth, as far beneath as earth is beneath heaven, into misty Tartaros (Theogony 717–725). Hesiod gives Kronos no speech and no defense; he simply falls, as Ouranós fell before him. The myth means that Greek cosmogony is written by the winners — each revolution calls the previous age a tyranny, and each tyranny believes its own propaganda.

myths.title: Lord of Abundance
myths.text: The Hesiod who damns Kronos also preserves the memory of his best age. In the Works and Days (109–126), the golden generation lived when Kronos reigned in heaven: mortals lived like gods, free of toil and grief, their earth spontaneously bearing fruit in lavish abundance; they feasted at ease and ‘died as if overcome by sleep’, and after death became pure daimones who walk the earth as guardians of justice. The Athenian Kronia kept this memory in ritual: a harvest festival of the twelfth of Hekatombaion in which, later authors report, slaves and masters dined together and social ranks dissolved for a day — Saturnalian inversion before the Roman Saturnalia gave it its famous form. The myth means that the devouring father and the generous king are the same god seen from different ends of time: every age of plenty is remembered as Kronos's, and every Kronos ends by eating his children.

myths.title: Kronos Beyond the War
myths.text: Not every tradition leaves Kronos in chains. Pindar, in the great second Olympian ode (68–77), describes the afterlife reserved for those who ‘thrice on either side of death have kept their souls from all unrighteousness’: they dwell in the Isles of the Blessed by the deep-eddying Ocean, ‘where fair-haired Rhadamanthys has his seat, and where Kronos is enthroned as king’ — a region of unplowed meadows, trees that drip frankincense, and flowers of gold. In this Orphic-tinged eschatology the fallen Titan is not the devourer but the just ruler of the happy dead, his crime swallowed by time as he once swallowed his children. Plato's Gorgias (523a–524a) keeps Kronos's memory in the myth of judgment, where Zeus ends the age of judging the living and institutes judgment of the dead — the old order of Kronos remembered as the era before justice became visible. The myth means that even the worst father can be redeemed by enough centuries: Kronos finally rules the one place where no son grows up.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Krónos with Saturnus (Saturn), an old Italic agricultural god whose temple stood at the foot of the Capitoline, and whose December feast, the Saturnalia — gift-giving, feasting, dice-playing, the temporary lordship of slaves — is the Golden Age staged as carnival (Macrobius, Saturnalia 1). The confusion with Khrónos, ‘Time’, began in Orphic and philosophical speculation and was complete by the Hellenistic age: Kronos, Time, and Saturn fused into the old man with scythe and hourglass who devours his children as the years devour our days. The Near Eastern comparative evidence is even older: the Hittite Song of Kumarbi (CTH 344, second millennium BCE) tells how the sky-god Anu is overthrown by Kumarbi, who bites off and swallows the offending organ — the direct eastern relative of Hesiod's scene, carried westward into Greek epic.
lore.culturalLegacy: Krónos haunts Western imagination as Father Time. Goya's Saturn Devouring His Son turned the myth into an image of mortality and madness. The planet Saturn bears his Roman name; Saturday (Saturni dies) is his day, and Christmas sits, by scholarly argument, atop the Saturnalia's feast-date. In fantasy and science fiction, ‘Cronus’ and ‘Kronos’ name doomsday weapons, time-travel devices, and tyrant-gods; the scythe of the Grim Reaper descends from Saturn's sickle through the Time-conflation. His name underlies the scholarly words ‘chronology’, ‘chronicle’, ‘anachronism’. Yet the original Krónos was also the lord of a lost age of plenty — a reminder that every devourer was once a generous king, and that time, which consumes all things, also made them possible.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Krónos is the god of the inevitable replacement. He does not ask permission to succeed his father, and he does not forgive his son for succeeding him. In this he is the most honest of the gods: he admits that power is temporary, that every ruler becomes the obstacle the next generation must remove.

But Krónos is also the god of the harvest, and the harvest is time made visible. The sickle cuts the grain because the grain has reached its hour. His tragedy is that he tried to stop the cycle he embodied. To name him Krónos is to remember that time cuts down even the one who holds the blade.
lore.archaeology: At Olympia the Hill of Kronos (Kronion) rises above the sanctuary; Pausanias (6.20.1) records that the Eleans honor the god on its summit, and the Kronia was celebrated there in connection with the games' founding legend. Votive material from the precinct links the site to the old couple Kronos and Rhea. In Athens the Kronia marked the height of summer with its licensed inversion. At Rome, the Temple of Saturn in the Forum — vowed in the early Republic, rebuilt by L. Munatius Plancus in 42 BCE — housed the state treasury and the god's image bound in woolen fetters loosed for the Saturnalia; its surviving columns still stand at the foot of the Capitoline.
